steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The lamp had gone out only once in Elias Morrow’s thirty-two years on the headland, and no ship had been lost for it. The sea had been calm, the sky clear as cut glass; no one but Elias and the gulls had even noticed that for a full thirteen minutes the Tower of Northfell had been blind.

He had never forgiven himself anyway.

Every evening, as the sun lowered into a rust-red smear, he made the same round: check the oil, inspect the prisms, wipe the salt film from the glass, listen to the wind testing the stones. The tower was old enough to creak in a storm and hum on quiet nights, a kind of breathing. Elias liked to imagine it did so in relief when he touched the walls, as though reassured someone was still there.

The keepers’ cottage, a squat lump of granite pressed into the cliff, shared the same smell year after year: paraffin, tea leaves, drying wool, and the faint iron tang of rust that never quite surrendered to paint. His boots lived by the door. His bed, narrow and stiff, faced the sea. There was a table, a chair, a shelf of novels with cracked spines, and a tin box he never opened.

The tides kept a better calendar than he did. Winter was the season of black water and invisible horizons, of waves that smashed themselves white against the rocks and threw spray all the way up to the lantern room. Summer brought haze that swallowed distances, and heat that made the slabs of the stair curl their own damp air upward.

People came twice a month: a launch from the harbor, men with crates and shouted jokes, letters in a pouch. Sometimes one of them would ask, in the light, clumsy way of people too polite to be direct, “You ever get lonely up here, Mr. Morrow?”

Elias would shrug. “Not when there’s weather.”

It was half an answer. Weather never stopped; it came in layers of cloud and wind and scent, full of small tasks and adjustments. Loneliness only had room to grow when the world went flat and fair.

On such days, he found himself listening for a second set of footsteps on the stairs that never came.

He could still hear them anyway.

The first time Elias climbed those stairs, he’d been twenty-two and full of the heavy, eager silence of a man who’d left more than he could carry behind him. The head keeper then had been a wiry woman called Bramwell who smoked foul little pipes and knew the names of the rocks like they were her children. Under her were two assistants: Elias and Jonah Pike.

Jonah had laughed the first time the foghorn sounded while Elias was in the yard. Elias, nearly jumping out of his skin, had turned to see Jonah doubled over, hands on his knees, light as if the wind itself found him amusing.

“You get used to it,” Jonah had said when he could breathe. “Eventually you’ll sleep through that beast. Or you’ll go mad. Either way, problem solved.”

Their days had filled with small rituals: shared mugs of tea at midnight in the lamp room when the sea was a blind thing beneath them; half-serious arguments about constellations; the battered deck of cards whose faces had been thumbed almost blank. When shifts overlapped, they moved around each other easily, a dance built of repeating circles, oil cans, charts, and the circular stairs.

One November night, a storm came in on a long, low growl. The barometer had been falling all afternoon in a way that made Bramwell pinch her mouth thin.

“Weather’s coming nasty,” she said. “Tie down everything that isn’t mortared. Check the lantern twice.”

By dusk, the sky had gone the color of bruised plums. The wind found new doors in the stone.

The radio crackled with small craft warnings. No sane captain would have been near the Northfell rocks that night. No sane captain, but not all captains had the luxury of sanity with schedules to meet and owners to please.

It was Jonah’s watch in the lantern room. Elias, below, was hunkered at the table, listening to the storm grind its teeth around the cottage, when the first call came through the radio. A voice, thin and ragged with static.

“—Mayday—trawler Erin—lost power—drifting…break…lights…?”

Bramwell’s hand shot out and snatched up the microphone. “Erin, this is Northfell Light. We’ve got you. Keep your head due east if you can. Can you see us?”

A pause, filled with hiss and the distant bellow of the horn.

“…Negative. Nothing. Black… Think we’re north of—”

The transmission dissolved.

Bramwell’s eyes were already on the ceiling, on the tower that rose through it. “Lamp’s fine,” Elias said. “I checked not an hour ago.”

“Check again,” she snapped.

Elias all but ran for the door, the wind punching it in toward him. Rain stung his face, horizontal. The tower loomed, a pale cylinder streaked with shadow in the strobes of lightning.

He took the stairs two at a time, hand skidding on wet stone where someone’s boots had tracked rain. Halfway up, the lamp flickered. Once. Twice.

Then it went out.

The darkness inside the tower was complete. Elias’s breath hitched. One heartbeat. Two. His hand shot to the rail, mind running ahead of his feet.

The backup. The wicks. The fuel. Jonah.

“Jonah?” he called, the word ripped away by thunder.

No answer. Only the thunder, and an odd, thin squeal from above, like metal protesting.

At the lantern room door, his fingers found the latch by feel. He shoved it open.

The great lantern, a towering array of lenses and metal, stood dark. The emergency lamp, smaller and stubborn as a stub of candle in a storm, had not been lit. One of the casement windows was open a hand’s width, rain knifing through sideways. A coil of rope lay unhooked from its cleat. The safety harness hung empty on its peg.

“Jonah?” Elias heard his own voice, high and pointless against the storm’s roar.

Lightning. For a fraction of a moment the sea outside was etched in white, the waves a field of jagged glass. He thought—he would swear to this later, in the gray room with the officials and their careful pens—that he saw a shape in that white, far below and too close to the cliff. Something in the water that was not water.

Then darkness again. The storm closed its hand.

The next few minutes existed in his memory as if viewed from somewhere above his own shoulder: him fumbling for the matches, fingers numb; the strike and flare; the smell of sulfur and oil; the hiss and podge as the emergency lamp caught and the lenses took that meager flame and flung it out over the water with all the stubborn power of glass and geometry.

The light returned. The horn bellowed. The tower, blind for only thirteen minutes, opened its eye again.

They never found Jonah.

It was assumed, later, that he’d gone out onto the gallery to check the shutters, been caught by a freak gust, a stray patch of slick stone. A simple thing. A misstep. The sea loved such missteps.

Elias knew only that the lamp had gone out on Jonah’s watch, for the first and only time in his career. That there had been no sign of struggle, no scorched wick or broken gear, only the quiet, methodical absence of light. As if someone had chosen, with steady hands, to extinguish it.

The Erin limped into harbor at dawn with a shredded net and a crew who swore they’d have ridden the rocks if Northfell’s beam hadn’t burned back into life when it did. Bramwell accepted the harbor master’s gruff thanks with a nod and a cigarette. Elias stood back, silent. His ears still rang with the horn and with the question that had bloomed in him like mold in the dark: How close had they come?

In the months that followed, the official questions flattened into paperwork. Jonah Pike: lost at sea, presumed drowned. An accident. A pity. His name carved, small and shallow, on the memorial stone near the harbor where widows left flowers that the wind eventually took.

Elias returned to the tower.

Now, years later, he still climbed those stairs, one hand trailing along the inner wall as if he could feel, faint and cool, the ghost of Jonah’s passing. Time blurred the edges of the man’s face in his mind—was his hair that dark? Did he laugh that loud?—but nothing could sand down the memory of that black circle where the lamp should have been.

He kept the safety harness oiled. He checked the fastenings of the casements twice when weather threatened. And sometimes, when the sea lay smooth and the stars were careless, he would lean on the rail of the gallery for a minute too long, and the wind would push insistently at his coat, and he would think of hands on a railing and a deliberate step forward into nothing.

He lived. The lamp burned. Ships passed and did not founder.

Decades blurred between storms.

On a spring morning that smelled of kelp and diesel, the harbor launch brought a journalist, all bright eyes and stiff notepad. She had the careful enthusiasm of someone on a human-interest assignment.

“Mr. Morrow? I’m writing a piece about the last manned lights on this coast. They’re automating most of them now, you know.” She gestured vaguely at the tower. “How does it feel to be nearing the end of an era?”

He poured her tea he knew she would not finish. The launch bobbed in its mooring below like a patient dog. Out at the horizon, a container ship moved, glinting.

“Feels like any other end,” he said after a moment. “Slow while it’s happening, sudden when it’s done.”

She smiled, pen ready. “Have you ever had any…dramatic nights?” she asked. “Wrecks, storms, that sort of thing? Something that made you feel what you do really mattered?”

Elias looked at her. Young. The kind of young that believed stories needed spikes of drama to be worth telling.

He thought of the Erin. Of the storm that had eaten Jonah. Of the thirteen minutes in which the world outside the glass had been utterly blind because a man had decided, so quietly no one heard, that he’d had enough of being a small, necessary cog.

He could say: Yes. He could tell her about the mayday, the thunder, the blackout. She would write it down: tragedy, peril, near-miss. The readers would murmur and turn the page, warmed by the confirmation that someone had once, in a romantic storm, held the line between disaster and survival.

“Once or twice,” he said instead. “But it’s the dull nights that matter more.”

She blinked. “How so?”

“Because no one remembers not dying,” Elias said mildly. “The ships that pass and never even know how close the rocks are. That’s the point, isn’t it? The lamp’s there so nothing happens.”

She hesitated, then wrote that down anyway. “Do you ever feel lonely?” she asked, as if it were compulsory.

“Not when there’s weather,” he said, and this time he heard Jonah in his own voice.

Later, after she’d gone and the launch had shrunk to a dot and disappeared behind the curve of the bay, he climbed to the lantern room again. Habit and, he would concede only to himself, superstition.

The room smelled of warm glass and old brass. Beyond the windows, the afternoon lay soft and blue, the sea repeating itself to the horizon.

In a corner, beside a brass vent that whistled faintly, sat the tin box he never opened. Bramwell had left it when she retired, sliding it onto the shelf with a grunt. “For when the light goes automatic,” she’d said. “If they don’t send anyone to relieve you, you’ll have to let yourself go.”

She’d winked at her own morbid joke and walked away, her boots coming down the stairs in a rhythm that, for a long time, Elias had listened to in his sleep.

The box had sat there through six governments, four different makes of radio, and a steady march of ships that had grown from rust-streaked freighters to enormous, clean-sided carriers. Engineers had come and gone, bolting new sensors to old stone, wiring quiet boxes that blinked green in corners. “Just in case,” they’d said once, years ago, “someone forgets to turn on the light.”

Elias had never forgotten.

Now, with the automation date set — a letter with precise language and a stamped signature lay folded in his desk — the box felt heavier in the room, its presence less theoretical. A joke that had waited patiently at the edge of conversation, suddenly pertinent.

He picked it up. The tin was cold, even in the gentle spring warmth. The lid came off with a soft, reluctant sigh.

Inside were keys. A spare to the tower door, which he already had on his ring. A smaller one, unfamiliar, with no tag. A folded sheet of paper, the creases deep and permanent.

His name was on the outside. Not Bramwell’s hand.

His thumb hesitated, then slid the paper open.

The writing inside was angled, impatient, a script he hadn’t seen in thirty-two years and recognized instantly all the same.

Eli—

If you’re reading this, I’m either dead or retired. If it’s the first, don’t get sentimental, it makes the gulls smug.

There isn’t a right way to leave this place. Bramwell says you walk down the stairs and you don’t look back. I don’t think I can do that. I’ve spent the last weeks trying out farewells in my head, but they all sound like lies when I get to the door.

So here’s the truth, since walls don’t gossip and tin keeps secrets.

I’m tired.

Not in the bones, though there’s that, too, from the damp and the stairs and wrestling with shutter bolts in the dark. Tired like a wick that’s burned so slowly it doesn’t know it’s short until someone lifts the chimney and sees there’s not much left.

I love it here. That’s the bitter bit. I love the beam cutting through fog like a promise. I love the way ships answer with a dip of their lights, as if they’re saying, “We see you seeing us.” I love the stupid gulls and the smart storms and watching you fall asleep in your chair with a book on your face.

But loving a thing isn’t the same as wanting to stay with it.

You, of all people, will understand that I think too much when it’s quiet. The silence up here can get under your fingernails. On fair nights it presses in like glass. I start thinking about how many men out there are steering straight because I’m up here turning a knob, and then I think about what happens if I don’t, if my hand slips, if the oil runs dry, if I forget.

We talk about duty like it’s a coat we put on, but living inside the word “if” every day wears a man down.

I went ashore last month, remember? Storm damage on the intake pipe, had to let the harbor boys ferry me. Do you know what I saw on the quay? Nothing special, which is why it hit me so hard. A woman haggling over fish. A child with a red balloon that kept trying to escape. A dog too old to jump up on a ledge, so it waited and barked until its owner lifted it. Ordinary things. No one on that stone knew or cared which direction the light turned that night. They took their own lives for granted, as if some huge hand wasn’t always hovering over them, deciding: rock or safe passage.

I realized I didn’t know how to stand in that market as a man who could walk away. Who would I be if I wasn’t someone whose absence might kill strangers?

It’s a ridiculous question, but ridiculous questions keep me awake more than the sensible ones.

So I’m leaving.

Not the way Bramwell did, with a handshake and a pension and a seat in the pub where people call you “Keeper” until the name wears thin. If I go that way, I’ll always be listening for this foghorn in every kettle’s whistle. I know myself that much.

By the time you find this, I’ll be down there somewhere.

Don’t get noble ideas about diving in after me. That’s why I didn’t tell you while I was still upstairs drinking your terrible tea. The rope will be unhooked. The window open. You’ll do your job and light the aux lamp because that’s who you are, and a ship will not hit rocks because of me.

You’ll think I’m selfish. You’ll be right. You’ll think I could have stayed for your sake. Maybe. But then I’d be staying because you needed me, and that’s just shifting the rocks, not getting out from under them.

If there’s any comfort in this, let it be that I chose my dark. So many don’t get the choosing.

Take care of the light for as long as it lets you. Then let it go. You are not the lantern.

You’re just the man who made sure it never went out—until you didn’t have to anymore.

—J.

P.S. That little key’s for the bottle I hid under the third stair from the top. If they haven’t found it by now, they never will. Have a drink on my poor judgment the day you leave.

Elias stood very still. The tower hummed around him, the glass ticking as the sun warmed one side more than the other.

He had built, over the years, all kinds of small, merciful lies about Jonah’s end. Accidents, missteps, sudden squalls. He had given the man back his balance in his imagination, if not in fact.

The letter took that from him and gave him something else: a choice. Not his own, but Jonah’s clear as a flare in the dark.

You are not the lantern.

Below, the sea folded itself against the rocks, again and again, practicing erasure.

That evening, when the sun brushed the horizon, Elias climbed the stairs for what he knew would be one of the last times. The automation team was due in a week. They would bring panels and manuals and a sense of inevitability.

At the top, he did what he had always done. He checked the oil, though the new electrics purred steadily. He wiped a smear from the glass with the corner of his sleeve. He looked out.

Lights pricked on along the invisible curve of the coast, small domestic constellations. Far off, another lighthouse’s pulse winked, on and off, like a slow heartbeat.

He reached under the third stair from the top, fingers searching the rough stone. They found metal, then glass. He brought up the dust-filmed bottle and turned it in his hand. The label had given itself to time. Inside, the liquid flashed amber when it caught the last of the sun.

Elias glanced at the letter on the table, at Jonah’s looping last line.

Outside, a ship moved steadily north, its own lights simple and sure.
